steps.text: Preheat oven to 450 degrees F (230 degrees C). Lightly grease a baking sheet with 1/2 teaspoon of lard.

Mix together the flour, salt, baking soda, and baking powder in a bowl. Grate the frozen butter and 2 tablespoons frozen lard into the flour mixture with a cheese grater; stir lightly 1 or 2 times to mix. With your fingers, make a well in the middle of the flour mixture, and pour the bacon drippings and buttermilk into the well. With just the tips of your fingers, stir lightly and quickly to just bring the dough together before the butter and lard melt. Dough will be sticky.

Scrape dough out onto a floured surface, and gently pat the dough flat. Sprinkle the top of the dough with flour, and fold it in half; pat down, fold again, and repeat until you have folded the dough 4 or 5 times. With a rolling pin, roll the dough out to a square about 1 inch thick. Cut the biscuit dough into rounds with a 2 1/2-inch biscuit cutter or the floured edge of a drinking glass by pushing straight down (twisting the cutter will seal the edge and keep the biscuits from rising). Lay the biscuits onto the prepared baking sheet so the edges just touch.
Bake in the preheated oven until risen and lightly golden brown, 15 to 20 minutes.

raw_recipe.headline: Greg's Southern Biscuits
raw_recipe.description: Limber up your biscuit-making fingers and try this vintage recipe that's been handed down for generations. Grandmas know the secret to great biscuits is to handle the dough as lightly as possible.

video.description: A fluffy, soft, and flaky delight to have with breakfast. Spread on jam, butter, honey, (or all three!) for a tasty addition to many meals.

review.reviewBody:
Disclaimer, This is my recipe. I just wanted to pass on some tips. First off. Stick to the recipe, please don't alter it, then rate it, as its no longer mine. 

Do not over work the dough, flatten out gently, dust lightly with flour, (will be sticky) pat gently and then fold again, repeat, you should only do it 4-5 times max, any more and your dough will comes out flat, dense, and chewy. 

If they don't turn out like that, you more than likely overworked the dough, or need fresh baking powder/soda 

These rise about an inch on avg.

Remember the key is, handle the dough as lightly and as little as possible. 

A Tip: To make buttermilk just add a 1 tbs of white vinegar to a cup of milk. Let sit for 5 minutes, and you now have buttermilk. 

To keep the lard/butter from clumping, grate directly over the flour moving it around as you grate and give a little stir if you see it clumping. 

BTW Grandma always sifted her flour, I did not, 

I've eaten a lot of country food. This is the best biscuits I've ever had. If yours don't turn out delicious, please try again, as something went wrong. It's worth it. Btw- These biscuits should be soft in the middle and have a very light crunch on the top. Grandma's words about biscuits, it largely comes down to feel and texture of the biscuit when it is kneaded perfectly with the right moisture to flour ratio and that comes only with a little practice. Enjoy! WARNING: this is NOT health food, Please judge solely on taste.

We were spending the night in the mountains with our kids and I promised biscuits and gravy for breakfast. Took everything with us - put the dry ingredients in a plastic bag and kept in the freezer along with the butter. Didn't have lard. Added the bacon grease and buttermilk to a jar. In the morning, cut up the frozen butter, mixed w/flour, added buttermilk. Patted the dough out, used my bench scrapper to fold so the dough stayed cold. Did the final pat out on parchment, cut with the bench scraper, transferred to a sheet pan and baked. You don't need gravy or butter. Tender on the inside and lightly crisp on the outside. This is the recipe I've been looking for. YUUMMMM!!

These are awesomely easy to make and they turned out beautifully. This is the first time that a buttermilk biscuit I made turned out like an actual biscuit and not like a hockey puck. I’d like to give the recipe owner credit for that, but I’m more if it’s this recipe or the new flour I ordered online to try my hand at making a buttermilk biscuit again. Those of us in the northern part of the country have no idea that the flour those in the south use is far different that the typical all purpose flour we can buy in the stores up here. The flour they use in the south has a lower protein count than ours. That results in a lighter “airy” biscuit. Using pastry flour (also has less proteins) or a brand like White Lily helps ensure that you don’t get hockey pucks to serve with your meal.

Nice biscuits interesting technique that works well and is fast! Two alterations: I used tenderflake & butter Also as suggested increased the baking powder. 
Overall a nice product, pleased to serve. 
Thanks for the technique. 

Updated:
I have applied a somewhat different technique. Once the mixture is turned onto the rolling surface: I press it into a 1 inch rectangle. Then with a pastry scraper, I cut the rectangle in 4. Next you pile the squares (tuck loose flour and scraped between layers) and press the mass down gently into a 6X9 rectangle one inch thick and then cut into 6 squares. I baked mine in a Well greased muffin pan. Buttery and crisp on the outside and tender layers inside. Mmmm

I did not have any lard and used butter and they came out just fine. I also experimented with making them into and angel biscuit to serve with strawberries and whipped cream...used butter instead of bacon grease for that (so now it is all butter) and added 1 tsp of yeast to the buttermilk/let it rise for an hour before baking. Awesome dessert biscuit! As posted along the way..the real secret is minimal handling of the dough.

These are the best biscuits that I have made in many years-if not EVER!!! We absolutely loved them! I live in the South, where lard is pretty easy to find, but I just couldn't bring myself to buy any, so I subbed cold shortening. I also used a little bit more butter than 2 Tbsp because of my preference for really buttery biscuits. However, the flavor that really amazingly stood out to me was the small (seemingly) miniscule tsp of bacon fat! The flavor imparted by that small amount permeated the entire biscuit! My only disappointment was that I only got 7 out of the recipe! Although these biscuits are quite an indulgence, this is my absolute go-to biscuit recipe going forward. I can't thank you enough for sharing this family gem with us Greg! Many blessings.

Very good. I change it up to what I think is a little easier due. to using less ingredients plus a better outcome (for me anyway). I use self-rising flour because it's pre-mixed to include a blend of hard and soft wheat as well as a leavening.

Finally! The southern biscuit recipe I've been looking for all my life. Two things, though: the dough was not sticky, it was gloppy; and needed more salt. Next time, I'll reduce the liquid to 3/4 C and add more if needed, and increase salt to 1 t. Thank you!

I was a little generous on the fats. I cut the biscuits into 9 squares as I'm too lazy to use the cup and re-roll scraps...'course, I didn't have buttermilk so used the next best thing.. vinegar and milk...

These were great! OK I did not follow the recipe to the letter. I did not freeze my butter and lard. They were just cold from the refrigerator. So I just cut them up into little cubes and used a pastry knife to cut them into the flour. My bacon fat was also cold so I cut that in as well. But the biscuits came out wonderful. Tall and fluffy and oh so good. This is the way I will make all my biscuits from here on.

To guarantee a flaky and layered biscuit, I pat out , cut and pan a first layer, Pat out the remainder. cut and butter a set of toppers for the first layer. Add the second cut, butter side down on the first layer. They bake up great with a two layer biscuit that always divides where you want it to. This dough works great. For a slightly drier biscuit that really soaks up the gravy, work the dough less. For butter and jam or jelly. work it a bit more to develop the gluten in the flour.

Grating the butter is a great idea. I just used refrigerator cold but did make sure to stir it around in the flour as I grated. Also, no kneading just folding 4 or 5 times is perfect. Now my grandma never rolled and cut a biscuit in her whole life. She taught me to pinch off a palm size piece dusted with flour and roll it into a ball. In my biscuit pan a generous amount oil. Grease both sides of my dough ball in the pan then give it a pat. Let each biscuit lightly touch. Attached picture is the results
Epic awesomeness! Didn't change a thing and achieved lovely results! Wow!
Idk, I haven't made them yet!

Phenomenally, flaky goodness! I used kosher salt to give wonderfully flavorful bursts of crunchy, salty, crystalline surprises throughout. I added two pinches of sugar, and used heavy whipping cream because I was out of buttermilk. Buttermilk probably helps to keep the biscuits from crumbling quite as much as they did with the heavy cream. These were fluffy, flavorful, and moist. I can’t wait to make them with buttermilk. Thank you for the recipe!

These are very similar to biscuits I learned to make, the difference being I always use only lard in biscuits, no butter, though I'll admit it can add some flavor. The addition of bacon drippings was new to me, and I totally love it! (As a Southerner, I believe bacon in anything gets a thumbs up!) I did want to note that in the video when the woman is using the cutter/glass she twists it, a BIG no-no! You said as much in the directions, though. I also always keep dipping the cutter/glass in flour as that helps keep the dough from sticking to the cutter/glass. How I WILL use butter is to melt a few tablespoons and, right as the biscuits come out of the oven, use a pastry brush to slather some butter on the tops. YUM!!
1 full cup of buttermilk makes it work idk why they thought only 3/4 cup would work but anyway
These are great biscuits! The kids love them!
